findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: West Wales region continuing to experience high levels of delayed hospital discharges affecting emergency care capacity
findings.detail: A multi-council performance audit review identified ongoing challenges in supporting timely discharge from hospital across Pembrokeshire, Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion and Hywel Dda Health Board. Audit Wales issued 15 recommendations on capacity, discharge planning, information sharing, policy development and scrutiny arrangements to support regional improvement.
findings.matters: Delayed hospital discharge typically reflects adult social care capacity constraints; this can drive future service cost pressures and demand volatility, affecting council financial planning and resilience.
findings.figures: 15 recommendations across four partner organisations; 4-council regional review
findings.quote: High levels of delayed discharges continue to impact urgent and emergency care services.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Council has significantly strengthened corporate risk management arrangements in recent years
findings.detail: Audit Wales found the council operates within an up-to-date risk management framework supported by a positive risk management culture. Four recommendations were made for further enhancement in risk appetite and tolerance, escalation and de-escalation criteria, and risk reporting.
findings.matters: Robust risk management is foundational to council financial resilience; strong governance frameworks support a lender's confidence in the council's ability to navigate financial pressures.
findings.figures: Four recommendations identified for further enhancement
findings.quote: Audit Wales found that the Council has significantly strengthened its risk management arrangements in recent years and now operates within an up-to-date framework supported by a positive risk management culture.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Audit identified improvements needed in capital accounting processes before final sign-off
findings.detail: Audit Wales identified issues in capital transactions and balances that were corrected before final accounts approval. Recommendations were made to strengthen capital accounting processes and improve the timeliness of future financial statements.
findings.matters: Capital is typically material on local authority balance sheets; control weaknesses in capital accounting raise questions about the strength of underlying accounting control frameworks.
findings.figures: Specific amounts not disclosed; issues corrected before approval
findings.quote: Recommendations have been made to strengthen capital accounting processes and improve the timeliness of future financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Pembrokeshire County Council - Annual Audit Summary 2025
findings.headline: Draft 2024-25 accounts delivered after statutory deadline but received unqualified audit opinion with no material misstatements
findings.detail: Audit Wales received the council's draft accounts on 12 November 2025, after the statutory deadline. Improvements were needed in capital accounting, but these were corrected. Subject to council approval, an unqualified opinion is intended, with audit completion scheduled for 16 October 2026.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence both in the reliability of financial statements and in the council's ability to meet financial governance timelines; late submission signals a process control issue.
findings.figures: Accounts delivered 12 November 2025, audit completion 16 October 2026
findings.quote: Audit Wales received the Council's draft accounts on 12 November 2025, after the statutory deadline. Whilst improvements were required in relation to capital transactions and balances, the accounts were found to be properly prepared and materially accurate, with no uncorrected misstatements.

findings.headline: Compressed timetable for 2025-26 and 2026-27 audits requires completion of two audit cycles within ten months; draft 2025-26 accounts due 23 November 2026
findings.detail: To recover from 2024-25 delays and meet statutory deadlines, the council must submit draft 2025-26 accounts by 23 November 2026 and receive audit completion by 31 March 2027 at latest. This allows preparation of 2026-27 accounts by the 30 June 2027 deadline. The auditor explicitly describes this as 'a challenging timetable' and notes success depends on consistent delivery of high-quality statements and working papers.
findings.matters: This signals whether the council has resolved the underlying capacity and process issues that caused 2024-25 problems. Success is uncertain—the auditor states the timetable is challenging. Failure to meet 2025-26 deadlines would trigger further delays, renewed governance concerns, and potential need to disclose financial control deficiencies.
findings.figures: 23 November 2026 draft submission target; 31 March 2027 audit completion target; two audit cycles in ten months
findings.quote: This is a challenging timetable, as two audit cycles will need to be completed within 10 months.

findings.headline: Supporting working papers inconsistent with accounts and difficult to follow; audit queries took significant time to resolve; significant additional audit costs incurred
findings.detail: The auditor paused fieldwork to allow officers time to resolve asset accounting issues. Finance team sickness contributed to delays in responding to audit queries, particularly on issues requiring external valuer or IFRS16 system supplier consultation. These quality and timeliness issues resulted in significant additional audit costs, which the auditor will discuss separately with the Director of Resources.
findings.matters: Working paper quality directly impacts audit efficiency and cost. Unbudgeted audit costs represent a call on council resources. More importantly, these operational issues indicate resource constraints or process gaps in the finance function that may affect financial control and the ability to deliver services.
findings.figures: Significant additional audit costs incurred (amount not specified); implementation date for improvements 30 June 2027
findings.quote: Supporting working papers were not always consistent with the accounts and were sometimes difficult to follow. Responses to audit queries took a significant amount of time, particularly where officers needed to consult with the external valuer and/or the external supplier of the IFRS16 system.

findings.headline: IFRS16 lease accounting standard implementation identified errors in external system methodology and calculations, requiring significant additional audit work
findings.detail: The council procured an external system and supplier to support IFRS16 Leases implementation from 1 April 2024. Significant additional audit work was needed because errors were found in the system's methodology and underlying calculations, requiring rework before lease arrangements could be correctly recognized in the accounts.
findings.matters: IFRS16 is a material accounting change across all councils. Implementation difficulties in year one often recur in future years. This signals Pembrokeshire may face ongoing lease accounting quality issues unless root causes are addressed, affecting future audit efficiency and financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: £2,131,000 Right of Use Asset balance adjustment; errors in system methodology and calculations identified
findings.quote: Significant additional work was required during the audit to ensure that all potential lease arrangements had been appropriately considered and that working papers were complete and producing accurate figures as we identified errors in the methodology and calculations used.

findings.headline: Property revaluation net decreased £17,961,000 due to incorrect asset classification and inappropriate valuation basis; opening PPE balances adjusted £6,160,000 for unowned or unrecognized assets
findings.detail: Large corrections were required to asset values. Revaluations were corrected downward by £17.96m after incorrect asset classification and valuation technique errors were identified. Separately, £6.16m of opening PPE balances required adjustment for assets not owned by the council or previously unrecognized. Capital commitments were also understated by £9.703m.
findings.matters: Corrections of this magnitude indicate either weak asset management systems or loss of control over the asset register. For a council managing a significant property portfolio, this signals governance gaps in asset accountability that may persist unless root causes are addressed.
findings.figures: £17,961,000 revaluation decrease; £6,160,000 opening PPE adjustment; £9,703,000 capital commitments understatement
findings.quote: A series of amendments have been made to the revaluation basis of assets, which has resulted in an overall net decrease in the revaluation figure of £17,961,000. These include amendments relating to the incorrect classification of asset additions resulting in incorrect valuation techniques being applied, and in other instances, the incorrect valuation basis being applied.

findings.headline: Accounts submitted 12 November 2025, five months after the 30 June statutory deadline; audit certification due 16 October 2026, eleven months after the 31 October statutory deadline
findings.detail: The council submitted accounts for audit significantly late and the auditor will certify nearly a year after the statutory deadline. The unqualified opinion is ultimately issued but the extended timeline reflects operational issues in account preparation and audit delivery that neither finance directors nor lenders would normally expect.
findings.matters: Timely financial reporting is fundamental to oversight and lender confidence. Extended delays of this scale signal either persistent capacity constraints or process failures in the finance function that may continue to affect future years and service delivery.
findings.figures: Submitted 12 November 2025 (deadline 30 June 2025); certification 16 October 2026 (deadline 31 October 2025)
findings.quote: The accounts were submitted to us for audit on 12 November 2025, which was after the statutory deadline of 30 June 2025. We are aiming to certify your accounts on 16 October 2026. This is later than the statutory deadline of 31 October 2025.

findings.headline: Auditor issued unqualified opinion with no material uncertainties identified on going concern basis
findings.detail: The Auditor General for Wales issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements. The auditor concluded that the going concern basis is appropriate and has not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the Council's ability to continue operations for at least 12 months.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion with no going concern issues is a baseline expectation, but material to a lender as confirmation that the auditor has identified no material misstatements or financial sustainability risks in the statements presented.
findings.figures: No financial thresholds apply; audit conclusion is unqualified
findings.quote: In my opinion, in all material respects the financial statements: give a true and fair view of the financial position of Pembrokeshire County Council as at 31 March 2025 and of its income and expenditure for the year then ended

findings.headline: Pension fund liability position improved by £89m to a surplus of £201m
findings.detail: The Council's actuarial valuation shows the Dyfed Pension Fund surplus increased from £112m to £201m. This reflects revaluation of fund assets and update of actuarial assumptions at the latest valuation date (31 March 2022).
findings.matters: Pension position improvement is positive for long-term financial resilience and reduces future employer contribution volatility, though a lender would note that the valuation is based on 2022 asset positions and actuarial assumptions that may shift at the next triennial revaluation.
findings.figures: Pension surplus 2023-24: £112m; 2024-25: £201m; improvement of £89m
findings.quote: The Council's future surplus in respect of pension benefits payable, compared to assets held, is £201m at 31 March 2025, based on the latest actuarial assumptions. This has increased by £89m from 2023-24.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure fell 9% from £96.629m to £87.995m
findings.detail: Year-on-year capital spending decreased by £8.634m. The paper provides no explanation for this reduction in the auditor's sections supplied. This may indicate slippage in capital programmes or reduced ability to fund planned investment.
findings.matters: Capital expenditure reduction is relevant to a lender assessing delivery capability and asset investment trajectory, especially where a council is managing a large asset base or has committed infrastructure programmes.
findings.figures: 2023-24 capital expenditure £96.629m; 2024-25 capital expenditure £87.995m; reduction of £8.634m (8.9%)
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure (Note. 11.1.2.1) 96,629 87,995

findings.headline: Social Care overspends of £6.521m in the year were contained only by underspends in other services
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £5.649m and Adult Services by £0.872m, totalling £6.521m. These overspends were absorbed by underspends of £710m in Education and £1.977m in Infrastructure, meaning the overall £2.0m underspend masks structural pressure in social care budgets.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender needs to distinguish between an underspend masking structural cost pressures and true cost control. Social Care trends are material to councils' long-term budget sustainability; overspends in both children's and adults' services in the same year suggest demand or cost drivers outpacing budget provision.
findings.figures: Children's Services overspend £5.649m; Adult Services overspend £0.872m; total Social Care overspend £6.521m; net Council position underspend £2.0m
findings.quote: SOCIAL CARE - CHILDRENS SERVICES 31,556 37,669 37,205 5,649  SOCIAL CARE - ADULT SERVICES 80,127 84,047 80,999 872

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account rent arrears increased 25% from £2.523m to £3.162m with arrears as percentage of total rent due rising 2.16%
findings.detail: The HRA rent arrears have grown by £0.639m year-on-year. The paper notes this represents a further increase, indicating a trend rather than a one-off event. The percentage increase relative to total rent due rose 2.16% on the prior year end position.
findings.matters: HRA arrears trends signal tenant payment capacity stress and collection risk; for councils borrowing on their housing stock, arrears escalation at this pace reduces the revenue certainty on which rental income projections depend.
findings.figures: Rent arrears 2023-24: £2.523m; 2024-25: £3.162m; increase of £0.639m; arrears as % of total rent due increased 2.16%
findings.quote: Rent arrears for current tenants at the end of 2024-25 was £3.162m, a further increase of £0.639m on the 2023-24 year end position. The rent arrears as a percentage of total rent due had increased by 2.16% on the 2023-24 year end position.

findings.headline: Council Tax arrears rose 49% from £8.384m to £12.506m in a single year
findings.detail: All age categories show increases, with arrears less than one year old rising from £3.218m to £5.508m. The paper notes that some increase is due to properties transferring from housing benefit to Council Tax, but the 49% overall increase is substantial and suggests emerging collection issues.
findings.matters: A lender assessing debt sustainability needs visible evidence of revenue collection management; this scale of arrears growth in one year indicates either temporary shock or collection performance deterioration that will affect cash flow and funding capacity.
findings.figures: Prior year arrears £8.384m; 2024-25 arrears £12.506m; arrears <1 year increased from £3.218m to £5.508m
findings.quote: TOTAL PRIOR YEAR ARREARS 8.384 12.506

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate fell from 96.59% to 95.10%, a decline of 149 basis points
findings.detail: Cash collected to 31 March 2025 was £106.797m against a collectable debit of £112.296m. This decline in the collection rate is material compared to the prior year performance. Business Rates collection also declined from 98.17% to 97.59%.
findings.matters: Collection rate deterioration signals emerging revenue cash flow risk; a lender would need to assess whether this reflects transient economic conditions or structural weakness in the collection function.
findings.figures: 95.10% collection rate (2024-25) vs 96.59% (2023-24); £106.797m cash collected against £112.296m debit
findings.quote: Cash collected to 31 March 2025 was £106.797m against a collectable debit of £112.296m. This represents an in year collection rate of 95.10% which was lower than the 2023-24 collection rate of 96.59%.

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Second homes properties increasing in total number but declining in number liable for premium, as exemptions rise faster than overall stock growth.
findings.detail: Total second homes increased from 4,483 to 4,559 (up 76), but those attracting the premium fell from 3,748 to 3,688 (down 60), as exemptions rose from 735 to 871 (up 136). The largest increase in exemptions was for planning-restricted properties (Class 6), which rose from 447 to 600.
findings.matters: The widening gap between total second homes stock and those liable for the premium suggests continued downward pressure on income even if the premium rate is unchanged.
findings.figures: Total second homes: 4,483 to 4,559 (+76); subject to premium: 3,748 to 3,688 (-60); exemptions: 735 to 871 (+136); Class 6 exemptions: 447 to 600
findings.quote: The overall number of second homes in Pembrokshire has remained relatively stable over the last year, increasing from 4,483 in October 2025 to 4,559 in August 2026. The number of properties attracting the second homes premium has reduced slightly from 3,748 to 3,688, whilst the number of properties qualifying for an exception has increased from 735 to 871.

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Ongoing uncertainty over classification of self-catering properties between council tax and non-domestic rates, with valuation office appeals still pending determination.
findings.detail: The Valuation Office review of self-catering property classifications continues, but the true position remains unclear as 'many ratepayers have appealed the decision to remove the property from the non-domestic rating list and the VO continues to experience a backlog'. Q1 2026-27 saw 44 properties move from non-domestic rates to council tax and 38 move in the reverse direction, indicating continued volatility.
findings.matters: The classification of self-catering units affects whether revenue is collected as council tax or non-domestic rates, creating uncertainty for both forecasts and service funding.
findings.figures: Self-catering units on non-domestic rates: 1,700 (Oct 2025) to 1,829 (Aug 2026); Q1 2026-27 transfers: 44 NDR to council tax, 38 council tax to NDR
findings.quote: The true picture is still unknown as many ratepayers have appealed the decision to remove the property from the non-domestic rating list and the VO continues to experience a backlog of determinations.

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Second homes premium reduced in successive years—150% in 2025-26 creating £2.3m budget pressure, then 125% in 2026-27 creating £1.3m pressure—with Director warning similar reductions could repeat.
findings.detail: The premium has been reduced from 200% down across two years in response to consultation pressure, particularly from second home owners and tourism interests. The Director of Resources explicitly flags the risk: 'This risk would be realised for a third time should a decision be made to reduce the second homes Council Tax premium %'. The current recommendation is to maintain the 125% level.
findings.matters: A pattern of reductions driven by stakeholder pressure demonstrates political vulnerability of this revenue stream; each prior reduction has directly worsened the council's budget position.
findings.figures: 2025-26 budget impact: £2.3m; 2026-27 budget impact: £1.3m; cumulative: £3.6m
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025-26 Budget and was realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget. This risk would be realised for a third time should a decision be made to reduce the second homes Council Tax premium %

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Second Homes
findings.headline: Council allocates 92% of discretionary second homes tax premium income to fund core services budget, against a £23.3m budget gap for 2027-28.
findings.detail: The council allocates the majority of the second homes premium to general fund services including homelessness (£2.05m), schools (£4.71m) and public realm maintenance. The premium thus funds elements of core services that otherwise would need to be covered by other revenue sources. The Director of Resources notes that a 25% change in the premium level would change the 2027-28 budget gap by approximately £1.4m.
findings.matters: Depending on discretionary, politically sensitive revenue to fund core services creates structural financial risk, particularly when budget pressures are large.
findings.figures: 92% allocation; £9.008m allocated to general fund in 2026-27; £23.3m projected funding gap for 2027-28; £1.4m swing per 25% change in premium
findings.quote: Based on the current allocation of 92% of the second homes Council Tax premium income to the Council's budget relating to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities, a 25% decrease in the premium would increase the funding gap for 2027-28 by circa. £1.4m

findings.paper_title: 5.1 - Council Tax Premium for Long-Term Empty Properties
findings.headline: Council experienced £3.6m budget pressures from prior reductions in second homes Council Tax premium and is managing £23.3m projected funding gap for 2027-28 partly through discretionary premium income
findings.detail: The Director of Resources reports that reductions to the second homes Council Tax premium—from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 (£2.3m pressure) and further to 125% for 2026-27 (£1.3m pressure)—created material budget pressures. The council uses premium income to fund £9.008m of general fund spending (2026-27), primarily on homelessness support (£2.05m) and schools (£4.71m). With a £23.3m projected funding gap for 2027-28, the cabinet recommends maintaining the long-term empty property premium at 300% partly to avoid a third budget pressure event. The Director explicitly flags reliance on discretionary premium income as a key budget risk.
findings.matters: The council is using discretionary Council Tax premium income to fund core services, and has already experienced two material budget hits when member decisions reduced those premiums. A lender needs to understand this structural vulnerability and whether the council has alternative funding strategies for the gap.
findings.figures: £23.3m projected funding gap 2027-28; £2.3m budget pressure 2025-26; £1.3m budget pressure 2026-27; £9.008m general fund allocation from premiums 2026-27; £2.05m homelessness allocation; £4.71m schools allocation
findings.quote: This risk was realised with the Council decision to reduce the Second Homes Council Tax Premium from 200% to 150% for 2025-26 creating an additional £2.3m pressure for the 2025-26 Budget and was realised again with the Council decision to reduce the premium to 125% for 2026-27 creating an additional £1.3m pressure on the 2026-27 Budget. This this risk would be realised for a third time should a decision be made to reduce the Council Tax premiums % for 2027-28 or to reduce its allocation to the Council's budget.

findings.headline: Council acquiring leasehold property from elected Cabinet Member at externally-valued market price of £85,000
findings.detail: Pembrokeshire County Council is proposing to acquire a three-bedroom leasehold maisonette in Hakin, Milford Haven through its Housing Revenue Account property buyback scheme. The property is currently held by an elected Councillor and Cabinet Member. To ensure transparency and independence given the related-party nature of the transaction, an external RICS valuer was specifically commissioned. The independent valuation, based on recent comparable sales in the locality, valued the property at £85,000. The council anticipates approximately £5,000 additional capital expenditure to bring the property into line with its housing standards. The property is held on a lease with approximately 88 years remaining.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders care about how councils manage related-party transactions and whether appropriate governance controls and independent valuations are applied to ensure fair market value and audit trail for acquisitions from elected members.
findings.figures: £85,000 valuation; £5,000 anticipated works; 88 years remaining lease term; £10 annual ground rent; comparable evidence: 13 Waterloo Square £85,000 (June 2025), 10 Stephen Street £82,500 (June 2026), 31 Observatory Avenue £83,000 (November 2024), 14 Stephen Street £90,000 (March 2025)
findings.quote: We understand that an external valuation has been commissioned to provide additional independence and transparency because the seller is an elected Councillor and Cabinet Member of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Council Tax Premium Consultation Report 2027-28 (final)
findings.headline: 52% of consultation respondents favour removing Pembrokeshire's 125% second homes council tax premium
findings.detail: Consultation of 1,629 respondents shows opposition to the second homes premium set for April 2027: 52% prefer no premium, 91% prefer rates of 100% or less, and only 3% support the maximum 300% rate. Sentiment has shifted increasingly toward lower or no premiums compared to previous consultation years.
findings.matters: Public opposition to a council-set premium indicates policy risk; any change in premium rates could materially affect assumed revenue.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Full comments received for council tax premium consultation 2027-28
findings.headline: Second home owners and holiday let operators report selling properties due to premium burden; property sales increasing rather than housing released
findings.detail: Multiple respondents state they are selling or considering selling properties because of council tax premium costs. Several note property listings have increased (not decreased) since the premium was introduced, contrary to stated policy goal of freeing up housing. Respondents describe switching away from longer family holiday bookings to short-stay Airbnb lets, forced business closures in hospitality, and reduced consumer spending in local service businesses. One property owner reports being charged £17,500 in backdated premium bills.
findings.matters: If the policy's stated aim is to free up local housing and the effect is property sales and reduced accommodation stock, the policy is achieving the opposite result and generating economic damage to tourism/hospitality sectors—material to understanding whether council's housing strategy is working

findings.committee: Policy and Pre-decision Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Policy OSC Review of Council Tax Premiums Sep 2026 (final)
findings.headline: Properties subject to second homes premium declined from 3,748 to 3,688 as self-catering properties reclassify with exemptions
findings.detail: While total second homes in Pembrokeshire increased from 4,483 (Oct 2025) to 4,559 (Aug 2026), the number subject to the premium fell from 3,748 to 3,688. This reflects reclassification of self-catering properties transferring from non-domestic rates to council tax, where they receive Class 6 (planning occupancy restriction) exemptions preventing premium liability. The number with Class 6 exemptions increased from 447 to 600.
findings.matters: The premium revenue base is eroding as growth in second homes is offset by exempt classifications, reducing the revenue-generating capacity of this discretionary source
findings.figures: 3,688 premium-paying properties (Aug 2026) vs 3,748 (Oct 2025); 600 Class 6 exemptions (Aug 2026) vs 447 (Oct 2025)
findings.quote: The majority of exemptions to premium at August 2026 relate to Class 1 (for sale) 121 properties (139 October 2025) and Class 6 (planning occupancy restriction) 600 properties (447 October 2025) due to self-catering properties transferring into Council Tax from NDR.

findings.committee: Policy and Pre-decision Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Policy OSC Review of Council Tax Premiums Sep 2026 (final)
findings.headline: 25% reduction in second homes premium would create approximately £1.4 million budget pressure for 2027-28
findings.detail: The paper quantifies the financial exposure from changes to premium income. If Council Tax premiums are reduced, this will have negative impact on funding for affordable housing and Enhancing Pembrokeshire initiatives and on the council's overall budget position. A 25% reduction in second homes premium would equate to approximately £1.4 million budget pressure for 2027-28.
findings.matters: Shows the council is dependent on discretionary premium income for general budget funding, creating material exposure if that revenue falls due to policy changes
findings.figures: c£1.4m budget pressure for 2027-28 (based on 25% reduction scenario)
findings.quote: As a guide, a 25% reduction in Second Homes Premium (with the % to support elements of the budget related to affordable housing and enhancing the sustainability of local communities remaining the same) would equate to a budget pressure of c£1.4m for 2027-28.

findings.committee: Policy and Pre-decision Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Policy OSC Review of Council Tax Premiums Sep 2026 (final)
findings.headline: One-year statutory exemption from second homes premium to be introduced from 1 April 2027, with Welsh Government consulting on reducing the 182-day letting threshold and introducing five new exemptions
findings.detail: Welsh Government will introduce a one-year statutory exception from the second homes premium when properties transfer from non-domestic to council tax from April 2027. The government is separately consulting on reducing the 182-day actual letting threshold for self-catering properties and introducing five new exemptions for specific property types including holiday parks, multi-unit developments, properties with planning restrictions, annexes within curtilage, and farm properties. Legislative changes are intended to take effect from 1 April 2027 following consultation closure on 23 October 2026.
findings.matters: These policy changes will reduce Pembrokeshire's discretionary council tax premium revenue in future years, directly affecting the council's budget funding
findings.figures: 1,829 self-catering units on non-domestic rates (Aug 2026, up from 1,700 Oct 2025); consultation deadline 23 October 2026; implementation date 1 April 2027
findings.quote: From 1 April 2027 a one-year statutory exception from the second homes Council Tax premium (Class 8) will be introduced with the aim of ensuring a stepped transition is applied on a consistent basis across Wales.

Council is embedding methodology into staff training to mainstream as 'business as usual'. No quantified benefit or investment cost figures provided.
findings.matters: Vanguard represents significant organizational change investment; peer councils assessing similar approaches would want to know quantified outcomes; undisclosed figures limit ability to assess transformation cost-benefit
findings.figures: Described as delivering 'significant financial savings over and above the initial investment' but specific amounts not provided
findings.quote: At its July meeting, the Board heard that Vanguard working is delivering significant financial savings over and above the initial investment, though the benefits should not only be considered in financial terms, but also in additional cost avoidance, improved customer outcomes and increased staff capacity due to reducing failure demand and removing duplication from processes.

findings.detail: Key staff absences interrupted progress on this priority transformation programme. findings.detail: The council attributes the social care underspend to preventions-focused programmes beginning to deliver outcomes. Edge of Care delivered 91% of 316 accepted children remaining at home with 86% sustained outcomes at 12 months, generating £4.3m cost avoidance. Step Up Step Down achieved 93% positive family-based outcomes generating £675k cost avoidance. The 'Blues' and 'Bouncing Back' resilience programmes served around 900 pupils across 7 secondary schools with measurable improvements in emotional well-being.
findings.matters: Demonstrates preventions investment translating into budget outturn improvement; material outcome for a major cost area relevant to council's medium-term financial sustainability

findings.headline: The Capital Financing Requirement figures reported in this outturn are subject to change following completion of IFRS 16 accounting standard implementation.
findings.detail: The council has not yet fully completed the work required to capture the full impact of IFRS 16 (Leases) for the 2025-26 accounts. IFRS 16 brings previously off-balance sheet leased assets onto the balance sheet. Implementation of this standard will increase reported long-term liabilities and may increase the council's borrowing need. The final CFR will be reported in the Statement of Accounts.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 implementation introduces material accounting restatement risk to reported prudential indicators. A lender assessing the council's borrowing capacity and balance sheet strength needs to understand that the CFR figures in this report are preliminary and may change materially once the full impact of leasing arrangements is captured.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream fell to 3.47% from 3.89%, moving further from the council's 5.30% affordability cap.
findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream improved year-on-year, indicating that the cost of servicing the council's capital programme is declining as a proportion of available revenue. The council has set a maximum capping level of 5.30% for the General Fund, approved by Cabinet in November 2023 and maintained for 2025-26.
findings.matters: This ratio measures the affordability and sustainability of the capital programme. Improvement in this ratio, combined with a cap that is closely monitored as part of annual budget setting, signals that the council is managing capital investment within sustainable bounds even under budget pressure.
findings.figures: 2025-26 ratio 3.47% vs 2024-25 ratio 3.89%; capping level 5.30%
findings.quote: In 2025-26 the ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream was 3.47% (compared to 3.89% in 2024-25).

findings.headline: A £25m market loan was refinanced from a 4.58% rate to 4.08%, reducing annual interest costs.
findings.detail: On 4 March 2026, the council transferred a £25m market loan from Barclays to Phoenix Life, securing a 50 basis point reduction in the coupon rate. The new facility extends the maturity to November 2045 with an initial three-year interest-only period before converting to capital and interest repayments.
findings.matters: Debt refinancing at lower rates reduces financing costs and improves the council's debt sustainability position. This activity demonstrates active treasury management and captures savings from market movements.
findings.figures: Original rate 4.58%, new rate 4.08%; original maturity November 2066, new maturity November 2045; principal £25m
findings.quote: On 4 March 2026, the Council's £25m market loan with Barclays was transferred to Phoenix Life. The original loan carried an interest rate of 4.58% and was due for repayment in November 2066. It has been refinanced with new borrowing of £25m at a reduced rate of 4.08%.

findings.headline: Gross external borrowing came in at £201.8m against a budgeted £303.6m, leaving the council with an under-borrowed position of £85.6m.
findings.detail: The council maintained an under-borrowed position by using cash reserves to fund capital needs rather than external borrowing, a strategy it describes as prudent given that near-term investment rates were lower than medium to long-term borrowing costs. The council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) fell to £289.1m against a budget of £376.0m, a reduction of £86.9m.
findings.matters: Substantial divergence from budgeted borrowing indicates either stronger-than-expected cash generation or reduced capital needs. An under-borrowed position signals the council holds reserve capacity but may also reflect drawdown of reserves. Both matter to lenders assessing balance sheet strength and liquidity.
findings.figures: Budgeted gross external borrowing £303.6m, actual £201.8m; under-borrowing £85.6m (30% of CFR); CFR budgeted £376.0m, actual £289.1m
findings.quote: During 2025-26, the Council maintained an under-borrowed position. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement CFR)), was not fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an inter im measure.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure delivered £122.2m against an estimate of £157.3m, a shortfall of £35.1m.
findings.detail: The council's capital programme came in 22% below the Q3 estimate, driven by higher levels of grant funding and slippage in the capital programme. This underspend affected the council's borrowing requirement, which came in at £35m against an anticipated need of £47m.
findings.matters: A material underspend in a capital programme signals either delivery challenges or planning variance, affecting both the council's cash position and its ability to complete planned asset investment. Lenders track this as a measure of the council's capital management capacity.
findings.figures: Estimated £157.3m, actual £122.2m; anticipated borrowing need £47m, actual £35m
findings.quote: While it had been anticipated that the Council would need to borrow £47m during 2025-26, higher levels of grant funding and slippage in the capital programme resulted in borrowing of £35m with repayment of debt amounting to £25.3m during the year.

findings.headline: Vehicles & Plant reserve accumulated to £12.6m for planned capital replacement

findings.matters: Reserves built deliberately toward planned capital programmes demonstrate financial planning and signal the council's capital strategy and funding sources to lenders.
findings.figures: Reserve: £10.975m (2024-25 opening) to £12.624m (Q3 2025-26); £2.898m appropriated to capital in 2025-26

findings.detail: In 2025-26, £1.738m was transferred from the Risk Management reserve to provisions, reducing the balance from £2.335m to £725k. The transfer represents identification of specific risks or liabilities requiring formal provisioning.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor emerging provisions and risk identification to assess forward liabilities and understand what financial commitments the council is formally recognising.
findings.figures: Risk Management reserve: £2.335m (2024-25 closing) to £725k (Q3 2025-26); £1.738m transferred to provisions in 2025-26

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account Capital Fund depleted to £0.6m from £3.4m
findings.detail: The HRA Capital Fund fell from £3.383m at the opening of 2024-25 to £607k by Q3 2025-26, with £8.825m appropriated to capital in 2025-26 alone. The fund is being systematically drawn down to finance HRA housing capital schemes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know how housing capital investment is funded and whether the council has identified replacement funding sources for this reserve as it approaches exhaustion.
findings.figures: HRA Capital Fund: £3.383m (2024-25 opening) to £607k (Q3 2025-26); £8.825m appropriated to capital in 2025-26

findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position, using reserves instead of long-term borrowing to fund capital spending

findings.headline: Schools in deficit reduced from 24 to 19 and fewer schools budgeting in excess of funding, showing improved financial discipline

Overall school balance declining from £1.515m to £0.990m but composition improving, reflecting enhanced financial management support and scrutiny.
findings.matters: Positive trend in school financial health demonstrates effectiveness of management interventions and contrasts with overall council overspend.
findings.figures: 24 schools in deficit 2025-26, 19 projected 2026-27, 47 schools overspending 2025-26, 32 in 2026-27, aggregate balances £1.515m to £0.990m

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap for 2027-28 could widen by up to £6m to potentially £23.3m due to inflation and lower Council Tax growth
findings.detail: Approved MTFP projected £17.3m funding gap for 2027-28 (most likely scenario). Inflation modelling since February suggests additional cost pressures of up to £6m. Council Tax growth now expected lower than 5% assumption in MTFP. Benchmarking revealing some services cost substantially more than peers or Welsh Government estimates, requiring detailed service reviews.
findings.matters: Material deterioration in medium-term financial position signals likely need for significant service changes or savings, indicating sustained financial stress.
findings.figures: £17.3m approved funding gap 2027-28, additional £6m potential increase, 5% Council Tax assumption now expected lower
findings.quote: As a result, some initial high-level modelling has been undertaken to establish the impact of potential cost increases. This has led to a potential increase in the projected funding gap of up to £6.0m.

findings.headline: Council Tax arrears increased 56% year-on-year to £19.479m; new collection regulations expected to further delay recovery
findings.detail: Prior year arrears rose from £12.506m to £19.479m in one year. New regulations effective April 2026 extend the period before enforcement (up to 12 reminders before summons vs 3 previously), expected to slow collection further. £5.5m of arrears relates to second homes and long-term empty property premiums; £2.1m is tied up in disputed NDR/Council Tax reclassifications awaiting Valuation Office decisions (12-month backlog).
findings.matters: Material deterioration in cash collection, regulatory change adversely affecting recovery, and disputed valuations create cash flow and revenue certainty risks lenders monitor.

findings.headline: School Additional Learning Needs overspend of £1.166m dependent on unconfirmed Welsh Government funding
findings.detail: Council rebased ALN budget for 2026-27 but demand has exceeded projections, with 388 learners requiring support against 265 budgeted. This creates £1.166m overspend (53% of total council overspend). Welsh Government's proposed supplementary budget including £40m for ALN was voted down; funding confirmation not expected until November 2026 at earliest.
findings.matters: Single-service overspend accounts for over half the council's total overspend and relies on external funding not yet approved, creating material budget risk.

findings.detail: After underspending by £5.6m in 2025-26, Q1 2026-27 is projected to overspend by £2.2m on £347.4m budget. The Director of Resources notes this reversal requires careful management. findings.matters: Sudden reversal from substantial underspend signals loss of budget control and emerging cost pressures requiring intervention.

findings.headline: Additional £2.4m Council Tax income collected, but £1.0m appropriated to General Fund reserve for potential VOA appeal refunds
findings.detail: Council tax income exceeded budget by £2.4m during 2025-26, driven by increased number of second homes properties qualifying for premium as a result of transfer from non-domestic rates and the 182-day occupancy threshold. The council recommends appropriating £1.0m of this to the General Fund reserve to cover likely refunds if VOA appeals are successful (approximately £2.1m of second homes premium arrears is subject to VOA appeals). The remaining £1.4m has been appropriated to the Initiative Fund. This reflects prudent reserve management but signals that the additional income is not sustainable.
findings.matters: A lender needs to distinguish between recurring income and one-off gains. This additional income is at material risk of reversal. The appropriation to reserves rather than one-time use is the correct treatment, but it shows income volatility.
findings.figures: £2.4m additional income; £1.0m appropriated to General Fund; £1.4m to Initiative Fund; £2.1m of arrears subject to appeal

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered at 78% of Q3 projection, with actual borrowing of £35m against budgeted £86.3m
findings.detail: Capital outturn was £122.188m against Q3 projection of £157.286m (22% slippage). Slippage attributed to market capacity constraints in delivering schemes, inaccuracies in project profiles from project managers, inflationary pressures on materials and labour affecting scheme viability, and environmental requirements (nutrient neutrality for Milford Haven schemes) causing planning delays. Actual borrowing was £35m in 2025-26 against budgeted £86.3m, and £17.86m in 2024-25 against budgeted £45m. The council notes borrowing rates remained above the target Treasury Strategy rate, prompting a shift to short-term borrowing to avoid committing to high levels of long-term debt.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether capital slippage reflects delivery capability, inflation shock, or false budgeting. The shift to short-term borrowing is a hedging decision that defers rate risk. This council is managing debt conservatively but not delivering planned capital.
findings.figures: £122.188m outturn vs £157.286m Q3 projection; £35m actual borrowing 2025-26 vs £86.3m budgeted; £17.86m actual 2024-25 vs £45m budgeted

Given that borrowing rates have remained above the target borrowing rate set in the Treasury Strategy, a prudent approach has been adopted to avoid committing to high levels of long-term debt. Short term borrowing has therefore been used to manage temporary cashflow pressures.

Staff are engaged with pre-court visits and court proceedings are planned for non-engagement cases.
findings.matters: The paradox of high collection rate with growing arrears suggests a concentrating problem: some tenants falling progressively further behind. This has implications for both welfare (vulnerable residents) and asset quality (bad debt risk).

However, a core group of accounts with significant arrears continues to grow, with debts increasing over time.'
